title: Recursion
tagline: Recursive definitions, base case, tracing and terminating recursive methods.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material for the CISCE ISC Class XII Computer Science syllabus (subject code 868), examination year 2027, Section B. The syllabus topic list was taken from the verified 2027 syllabus; the explanations, examples and questions here are original and were not taken from any board examination paper, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Recursion is the technique of solving a problem by breaking it into smaller versions of the same problem. A recursive method calls itself, and each call works on a smaller input until a stopping condition is reached. When that happens correctly, the calls stop growing and the results are combined on the way back. When it does not, the method keeps calling itself until the program runs out of space for more calls. This chapter develops the idea from the ground up: what a recursive definition is, what a base case is and why every recursive method needs one, how the call stack grows and shrinks during a recursive computation, and how to trace both the calls going down and the results coming back up. It also covers the common mistakes that make recursion fail and the kinds of problems for which recursion is a natural fit.

Explain how the call stack grows with each recursive call and shrinks as calls return.

blocks.text: Recursion is the idea of defining a problem in terms of a smaller version of itself. A recursive method is one that calls itself. That sounds circular, and if nothing changed between the call and the recursive call it would be. The key is that each recursive call works on a smaller or simpler version of the original problem, until the problem becomes so small that the answer can be given directly. That direct answer is the base case.

A recursive solution always has two parts. The base case is the smallest version of the problem whose answer is known immediately, so no further recursive calls are needed. The recursive case is where the method calls itself on a smaller input and combines the result with the current step. If either part is missing, the method does not work: without a base case it never stops, and without a recursive case that moves toward the base case it never reaches the base case.

items: A recursive method calls itself.
The base case is the stopping condition that does not call itself.
The recursive case reduces the problem toward the base case.
Each recursive call is a fresh invocation with its own parameters and local variables.
Recursion is natural for problems with a self-similar structure.

items.meaning: The condition that stops further recursive calls and returns a direct answer.
The part of the method where it calls itself on a smaller input.
The stack of active method calls; each call adds a frame and each return removes one.

blocks.text: The base case is the most important part of a recursive method, because it is what prevents infinite recursion. A good base case is easy to recognise and covers the smallest meaningful input. For a method that computes the factorial of a positive integer, the natural base case is n equal to 1, or n less than or equal to 1, because the factorial of 1 is 1 and there is no smaller positive integer that makes sense to call the method on. Once the base case returns, the recursive calls can begin to return their results back up the chain.

The recursive case must reduce the problem in a way that eventually reaches the base case. For factorial, the recursive case is n times factorial of n minus 1. Each call passes a smaller n, and because n decreases by 1 each time, it eventually reaches the base case. If the recursive call passed the same n, or a larger n, or did not change the input at all, the base case would never be reached and the method would call itself forever until it ran out of stack space.

items.text: Factorial with a clear base case and recursive case.
items.note: static int factorial(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); }. The base case is n <= 1; the recursive case is n * factorial(n - 1).

items.text: A broken recursive power method that never reaches its base case.
items.note: static int power(int b, int e) { return b * power(b, e); }. The exponent e never decreases, so the base case is never reached. Each call waits for another call with the same e.

items.text: A correct recursive power method using a base case of e == 0.
items.note: static int power(int b, int e) { if (e == 0) return 1; return b * power(b, e - 1); }. Now e decreases by 1 each call until it reaches 0.

items: Choose a base case that is simple and obviously correct.
Make sure the recursive case always moves toward that base case.
Check that every possible input eventually reaches the base case.
Do not write a recursive call that passes unchanged data unless that data is already the base case.
Beware of methods with more than one recursive call, each of which must also move toward a base case.

learn.title: How the call stack works in recursion

blocks.text: Every method call in Java uses the call stack. When a method is called, a new frame is pushed onto the stack to hold its parameters and local variables. When the method returns, its frame is popped. In a recursive method, each recursive call adds another frame on top of the previous one, so the stack grows during the recursive descent and shrinks again during the return. That is why recursion uses extra space: the maximum number of simultaneous frames is the maximum depth of the recursion.

Tracing recursion means following both directions. On the way down, you follow the sequence of calls into smaller and smaller inputs until the base case is reached. On the way back up, you follow the return values as each frame computes its result from the value it got back. A common mistake is to trace only the calls and forget the returns, but the returns are where the actual answer is built.

items.text: Trace factorial(4) for factorial(n) = n * factorial(n - 1) with factorial(1) = 1.
items.note: Calls: factorial(4) -> factorial(3) -> factorial(2) -> factorial(1). Returns: 1 -> 2 -> 6 -> 24. The result is 24.

items.text: Trace sum of digits of 253 for sumDigits(n) = n % 10 + sumDigits(n / 10) with base case n < 10 returning n.
items.note: sumDigits(253) = 3 + sumDigits(25); sumDigits(25) = 5 + sumDigits(2); sumDigits(2) = 2 (base). Returns: 2 -> 7 -> 10.

items.text: Trace fib(4) for fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) with fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1.
items.note: The call tree branches at each step. fib(4) = fib(3) + fib(2); fib(3) = fib(2) + fib(1); fib(2) = fib(1) + fib(0). The base-case returns come from fib(1) and fib(0). The final value is 3.

items: Each call gets its own copy of parameters and local variables.
The call stack grows during the recursive descent and shrinks on the way back.
Trace both the calls and the returns.
For branching recursion such as Fibonacci, the calls form a tree rather than a single chain.
The maximum stack depth is the maximum number of active calls at any moment.

blocks.text: Writing a recursive method is easiest when you start by identifying the base case and then asking how a larger input can be built from the answer for a smaller input. That smaller-input relationship is the heart of the recursive case. Once you have it, the method is usually short. The danger is that the short method hides the complexity of what is happening on the stack, so it is worth tracing a small example by hand before declaring the method correct.

items.text: Recursive sum of the first n positive integers.
items.note: static int sum(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n + sum(n - 1); }. Base case n <= 1 returns 1; recursive case adds n to sum(n - 1).

static String reverse(String s) { if (s.length() <= 1) return s; return reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0); }. Base case is a string of length 1 or empty; recursive case puts the first character after the reversed remainder.

items.text: Recursive binary search on a sorted array.
items.note: static int binarySearch(int[] arr, int key, int low, int high) { if (low > high) return -1; int mid = (low + high) / 2; if (arr[mid] == key) return mid; if (key < arr[mid]) return binarySearch(arr, key, low, mid - 1); return binarySearch(arr, key, mid + 1, high); }. Base case is low > high; recursive case halves the search range.

items: State the base case first, before the recursive case.
Make the recursive case reduce the problem toward the base case.
Keep the recursive step simple and check it on paper.
For binary search, ensure the range shrinks each call, otherwise the base case may never be reached.
For string recursion, watch the substring bounds carefully.

learn.title: Common mistakes and when to use recursion

blocks.text: The most frequent recursion mistakes are missing the base case, failing to move toward the base case, and off-by-one or bounds mistakes in the recursive call. A missing base case causes infinite recursion and a StackOverflowError. A recursive call that does not reduce the problem causes the same outcome, even if a base case exists on paper. Bounds mistakes are common when the recursion depends on indices, because an incorrect midpoint or range can leave the recursion stuck.

Recursion is a good fit when the problem has a natural self-similar structure, such as factorial, reversing, tree traversal, or divide-and-conquer search. It is a poor fit when the recursion depth is large and iteration would be simple, or when the extra stack space is a real concern. In board work, the point is usually not to choose recursion for performance but to show that you understand how it works and how to trace it.

items.text: A recursive method with no base case eventually causes StackOverflowError.
items.note: Each call adds a frame; without a base case the frames never stop accumulating.

items.text: A recursive call that passes the same argument each time also causes StackOverflowError.
items.note: If factorial(n) calls factorial(n) again, the argument never shrinks and the base case is never reached.

items.text: Recursion is natural for tree traversal but iteration may be clearer for a simple loop.
items.note: Use recursion when it makes the structure of the problem clearer, and iteration when the iterative solution is equally clear and the depth could be large.

items: Missing base case leads to infinite recursion.
A recursive call that does not move toward the base case also causes infinite recursion.
Off-by-one and bounds errors are common in recursive index-based methods.
Recursion uses extra stack space proportional to its depth.
Prefer recursion when the structure is self-similar; prefer iteration when the iterative solution is clear and the depth could be large.

keyPoints: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a smaller version of itself and a base case.
Every recursive method needs a base case that stops further calls.
The recursive case must move toward the base case, or the method never stops.
Each recursive call has its own parameters and local variables.
The call stack grows during the recursive descent and shrinks on the way back.
Tracing recursion means following both the calls down and the returns up.
Factorial, string reversal, sum of digits and binary search are common recursive examples.
Binary search is recursive when the search range is halved each call and the base case is an empty range.
Prefer recursion for self-similar problems and iteration when the iterative solution is clear and depth matters.

vocabulary.meaning: A method calling itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem.
The condition that stops further recursive calls and returns a direct answer.
The part of a recursive method that calls itself on a smaller input.

questions.prompt: The part of a recursive method that stops further recursive calls is called the:
questions.answer: B) base case
questions.explanation: The base case stops further recursion and returns a direct answer.

questions.prompt: What happens if a recursive method has no base case?
options: D) It compiles but is slower
questions.answer: C) It causes StackOverflowError
questions.explanation: Without a base case the method calls itself forever and exhausts the stack.

questions.prompt: Each recursive call in Java gets its own:
options: A) copy of the caller's fields
B) copy of the parameters and local variables
C) copy of the entire object
questions.answer: B) copy of the parameters and local variables
questions.explanation: Each call has its own frame with its own parameters and local variables.

questions.prompt: The factorial of 1 is usually taken as the:
questions.answer: B) base case
questions.explanation: Factorial(1) = 1 is the natural stopping point for a factorial recursion.

questions.prompt: In recursive factorial of n, what is the typical recursive case?
questions.answer: B) n * factorial(n - 1)
questions.explanation: The recursive case multiplies n by the factorial of the next smaller number.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the call stack during recursion is true?
options: A) Each call shares the same frame
B) The stack shrinks on the way down
C) The stack grows on the way down and shrinks on the way back
D) The stack only grows for iterative methods
questions.answer: C) The stack grows on the way down and shrinks on the way back
questions.explanation: Each recursive call adds a frame on the way down, and frames are removed on the way back.

questions.prompt: Why does factorial(n) = n * factorial(n) fail?
options: A) It has no return type
B) It never moves toward the base case
C) It uses the wrong operator
questions.answer: B) It never moves toward the base case
questions.explanation: The recursive call repeats the same argument, so the base case is never reached.

questions.prompt: In recursive binary search, the base case is usually:
questions.answer: B) low > high
questions.explanation: When the range is empty, the search cannot continue and returns not found.

questions.prompt: The extra space used by recursive factorial(n) is typically:
questions.answer: C) O(n)
questions.explanation: Up to n frames can be active before the base case returns.

questions.prompt: Recursive binary search extra stack space is typically:
questions.answer: B) O(log n)
questions.explanation: Each call halves the range, so the depth is proportional to log n.

questions.prompt: A recursive method calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same blank.
questions.answer: problem
questions.explanation: Recursion is about solving a smaller version of the same problem.

questions.prompt: The condition that does not call itself is called the blank case.
questions.answer: base
questions.explanation: The base case stops further recursion.

questions.prompt: If a recursive method calls itself with the same argument each time, it will eventually cause a blank.
questions.answer: StackOverflowError
questions.explanation: Infinite recursion exhausts the call stack.

questions.prompt: In recursion, the phase in which calls go deeper is called the blank.
questions.answer: descent
questions.explanation: Recursive descent is the phase where calls go toward the base case.

questions.prompt: Explain why every recursive method needs a base case.
questions.answer: A recursive method calls itself. Without a base case, the calls never stop, because there is no condition that returns a value without making another call. The result is infinite recursion and eventually a StackOverflowError.
questions.explanation: The mark is for linking the base case to stopping the recursion.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the recursive case and the base case.
questions.answer: The base case is the simplest input whose answer is given directly, without another recursive call. The recursive case is where the method calls itself on a smaller input and uses that result to build the answer for the current input.
questions.explanation: The mark is for contrasting the direct answer with the self-referential step.

questions.prompt: Explain why tracing recursion means tracing both the calls and the returns.
questions.answer: The calls show how the problem is broken down into smaller calls until the base case is reached. The returns show how each call uses the value returned by its recursive call to build the final answer. If you trace only the calls, you miss how the result is actually built.
questions.explanation: The mark is for showing that the answer is built on the way back up.

questions.prompt: Write a recursive method to find the sum of the first n positive integers, and trace sum(4).
questions.answer: static int sum(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n + sum(n - 1); }. Trace: sum(4) = 4 + sum(3); sum(3) = 3 + sum(2); sum(2) = 2 + sum(1); sum(1) = 1. Returns: 1 -> 3 -> 6 -> 10.
questions.explanation: The mark is for correct code and a correct trace including the returns.

questions.prompt: Write a recursive method to reverse a string, and trace reverse("abc").
questions.answer: static String reverse(String s) { if (s.length() <= 1) return s; return reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0); }. Trace: reverse("abc") = reverse("bc") + 'a'; reverse("bc") = reverse("c") + 'b'; reverse("c") = "c". Result: "cba".
questions.explanation: The mark is for correct code and a correct trace including the returns.

questions.prompt: A student writes static int power(int b, int e) { return b * power(b, e); }. Identify the defect and fix it.
questions.answer: The defect is that e never decreases, so the base case is never reached. Fix it by adding a base case for e == 0 returning 1 and using power(b, e - 1) in the recursive case: static int power(int b, int e) { if (e == 0) return 1; return b * power(b, e - 1); }
questions.explanation: The mark is for identifying the missing reduction and supplying a correct fix with a base case.

questions.prompt: Explain why recursive binary search must reduce the search range each call. What happens if it does not?
questions.answer: Binary search works by halving the range of possible positions. If the recursive call does not reduce the range, the method may call itself on the same range forever, never reaching the empty-range base case. That leads to infinite recursion and StackOverflowError.
questions.explanation: The mark is for linking range reduction to termination and to the base case.

questions.prompt: Compare recursion and iteration for computing the sum of the first n integers. Which would you prefer and why?
questions.answer: Both can work. Iteration uses a loop and O(1) extra space. Recursion uses a call stack of depth n and O(n) extra space, but can express the sum as n + sum(n - 1) directly. For this simple problem, iteration is usually preferable because it is simple and uses less space, unless the self-similar structure is the point being tested.
questions.explanation: The mark is for a sensible comparison and a justified preference.

questions.prompt: Write a recursive binary search method on a sorted int array, and trace the search for 7 in [2, 4, 7, 9, 12].
questions.answer: static int search(int[] arr, int key, int low, int high) { if (low > high) return -1; int mid = (low + high) / 2; if (arr[mid] == key) return mid; if (key < arr[mid]) return search(arr, key, low, mid - 1); return search(arr, key, mid + 1, high); }. Trace: mid = 2, arr[2] = 7, found at index 2.
questions.explanation: The mark is for correct code and a correct short trace showing the match on the first midpoint.
